Why dense vectors?
Short vectors may be easier to use as features in machine learning (fewer weights to tune)
Dense vectors may generalize better than explicit counts
Dense vectors may do better at capturing synonymy:

tree.name: Bag of Words
tree.content: Bag of Words is a text representation that counts word occurrences ignoring order and grammar.

details.content: Bag of Words represents a document as a multiset of its words.
Bag of Words ignores word order, leading to loss of syntactic information.

tree.name: Co-occurrence Matrix
tree.content: Co-occurrence Matrix records how often pairs of words appear together within a context window.

details.content: Co-occurrence Matrix captures word association frequencies across a corpus.
Co-occurrence Matrix can become extremely large for big vocabularies.

tree.name: TF-IDF
tree.content: TF-IDF weights terms by frequency in a document and inverse document frequency across the corpus.

details.content: tf‑idf(i, j) = tf(i, j) × log(N / df(i))
TF-IDF reduces the impact of common words and highlights discriminative terms.

tree.name: One-hot Vector
tree.content: One-hot Vector encodes each word as a binary vector with a single high dimension.

details.content: One-hot Vector for "man" in a 9‑word vocabulary is [1,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0].
One-hot Vector creates high‑dimensional sparse representations.

tree.name: Dense Vector
tree.content: Dense Vector is a low‑dimensional continuous representation where most elements are non‑zero.

details.content: Dense Vectors may generalize better than explicit counts.
Dense Vectors aim to capture synonymy between words like car and automobile.

tree.name: Sparse Vector
tree.content: Sparse Vector is a high‑dimensional representation with many zero entries, typical of TF‑IDF or one‑hot.

details.content: Sparse Vectors are long (|V| = 20 000–50 000) and contain mostly zeros.
Sparse Vectors increase memory usage and computational cost.

tree.name: Word2vec
tree.content: Word2vec learns dense word embeddings using shallow neural networks such as CBOW or Skip‑gram.

details.content: Word2vec produces short (50–1000) dense vectors for each word.
Word2vec embeddings improve performance on downstream NLP tasks.

tree.name: CBOW
tree.content: CBOW predicts a target word from its surrounding context using averaged context vectors.

details.content: CBOW uses the one‑hot representation of context words as input x_i.
CBOW aims to maximize the probability of the correct target word y_i.

tree.name: Skip-gram
tree.content: Skip‑gram predicts surrounding context words from a single target word using its embedding.

details.content: Skip‑gram trains word vectors by maximizing likelihood of context words given the target.
Skip‑gram can be slower to train on very large vocabularies.

tree.name: Softmax Function
tree.content: Softmax Function converts raw scores into a probability distribution over the vocabulary.

details.content: softmax(z_i) = exp(z_i) / Σ_j exp(z_j)
Softmax Function is used in CBOW and Skip‑gram to model word probabilities.

tree.name: GloVe
tree.content: GloVe learns word embeddings by factorizing a global word‑co‑occurrence matrix.

details.content: GloVe offers fast training and stable quality on large datasets.
GloVe requires a lot of memory and is sensitive to learning‑rate initialization.

tree.name: FastText
tree.content: FastText extends word embeddings with subword information using character n‑grams.

details.content: FastText performs well with rare words because it incorporates n‑gram features.
FastText requires more memory due to character‑based storage.

tree.name: ELMo
tree.content: ELMo generates contextualized word embeddings using deep bidirectional language models.

details.content: ELMo provides better semantic representation than static embeddings like Word2vec.
ELMo requires more memory because it stores character‑based representations.
